flashcards.q: What is the single architectural difference between an encoder (BERT) and a decoder (GPT) Transformer block?
flashcards.a: The attention mask. Decoders use a causal mask so token i only attends to tokens 0..i (needed for autoregressive generation). Encoders use no mask, so every token attends to every other token bidirectionally.

flashcards.q: BERT has two pretraining objectives. Which one turned out not to matter, and what replaced/removed it?
flashcards.a: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) turned out not to matter — RoBERTa dropped it entirely, trained longer on more data with bigger batches, and matched or beat BERT. MLM (masked language modeling) is the objective that does the real work.

flashcards.q: Why does mean pooling usually beat [CLS] pooling for sentence embeddings on a non-fine-tuned BERT checkpoint?
flashcards.a: [CLS]'s only pretraining signal was NSP, a weak, largely-useless objective, so its raw embedding was never optimized to summarize sentence meaning. Mean pooling aggregates every token's contextual embedding instead of relying on one under-trained token.

flashcards.q: When is [CLS] pooling actually the right choice?
flashcards.a: After fine-tuning a classification head directly on top of [CLS] for a specific task — that fine-tuning is what makes the token's representation meaningful.

flashcards.q: State the bi-encoder vs cross-encoder difference precisely, in terms of what's precomputable.
flashcards.a: A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, so document vectors are precomputed offline and search is O(1)/query via ANN lookup. A cross-encoder feeds query+document jointly through one model, so the score depends on both together and cannot be precomputed — it costs O(n) full forward passes for n candidates.

flashcards.q: Give the rough latency numbers: ANN search over 10M docs vs cross-encoder reranking 100 candidates vs cross-encoder over the full 10M corpus.
flashcards.a: ANN search over 10M docs: single-digit-to-low-double-digit ms. Cross-encoder reranking 100 candidates: ~50-100ms on GPU. Cross-encoder over the full 10M corpus: on the order of hours per query (10M forward passes) — never done in practice.

flashcards.q: Why can't a cross-encoder's document-side computation be cached across different queries?
flashcards.a: Because attention runs jointly across query and document tokens through every layer, so the document's internal representations are influenced by the specific query tokens attending into them — there's no clean document-only intermediate state to freeze and reuse.

flashcards.q: How does ColBERT's late interaction relate to bi-encoders and cross-encoders?
flashcards.a: ColBERT keeps a per-token embedding for query and document (precomputed independently, like a bi-encoder) and scores with MaxSim (best-matching document token per query token, summed). It recovers token-level precision closer to a cross-encoder while staying precomputable, at the cost of storage scaling with total token count.

flashcards.q: Name four production tasks where a fine-tuned encoder beats a generative LLM, and roughly how much cheaper/faster.
flashcards.a: Classification, NER, retrieval embeddings, and moderation. Encoders run roughly 15-250x faster and 20-200x more cost/energy-efficient than an LLM prompted for the same fixed-label task, at equal or better accuracy.

flashcards.q: What determines whether a task should use an encoder or a decoder-based LLM?
flashcards.a: The shape of the output. Fixed labels, embeddings, or bounded extraction want an encoder (one forward pass, deterministic bounded output space). Open-ended generation, reasoning, or tasks needing natural-language justification want a decoder/LLM.

flashcards.q: What did ModernBERT change relative to the original 2018 BERT architecture?
flashcards.a: Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead of learned absolute positions, Flash Attention, alternating local/global attention layers, GeGLU activations, and an 8192-token context window, trained on 2T tokens of text and code — decoder-side advances retrofitted onto the encoder-only architecture.

flashcards.q: Why is BERT structurally unable to generate text the way GPT does?
flashcards.a: Bidirectional attention means every position already has access to the full sequence including future tokens, so there is no well-defined next-token distribution conditioned only on the past — the core mechanism autoregressive generation requires.

flashcards.q: A reranking pipeline's p99 latency blows the budget. What's the highest-leverage fix?
flashcards.a: Shrink the shortlist size fed to the cross-encoder (e.g. rerank top 20-50 instead of top 200-500) — cross-encoder cost is linear in candidate count, so this is almost always more effective than optimizing the model itself.

flashcards.q: What's the architectural difference between BERT (encoder-only) and T5 (encoder-decoder)?
flashcards.a: T5 has a bidirectional encoder that processes input once, plus a causal decoder that autoregressively generates output while cross-attending into the encoder output — built for seq2seq tasks with variable-length output. BERT has no decoder and cannot generate new token sequences; it produces labels, spans, or vectors.
